Sigmund Freud, a neurologist by training, revolutionized the way complex mental functions and their respective pathologies were studied in the early 20th century. From a simplistic interpretation in which aberrant mental processes could be explained by localizing damage to brain regions, Freud hypothesized that abnormal processes could also be caused by emotional variables with subjective meaning. Psychoanalysis became Freud's original method to study the relation between behavioral disturbances and the human subjective experience. Since then, medical knowledge of the brain has become increasingly specialized and has given rise to different disciplines, such as neuroscience, which in turn has made the separation between science and psychoanalysis an ever-increasing challenge. Freud (1910/1957) himself saw the important interconnection between the mind and the brain, urging psychoanalysts to “… never forget that the mental is based on the organic,” and thus remained hopeful that one day his original model of the mind could be correlated with brain functions. 274

It seems to be an extraordinary moment, a moment of resonance and revisiting, for this journal to publish Clara Thompson's 1955 address to the Harry Stack Sullivan Society, the candidate group at White. Reading a paper not generated from a computer, in old familiar typescript, bearing the particular look of manuscripts from the mid-20th century, I tumbled to the past and back to the present again, in an often very unsettling way. Thompson's lecture should come with a WARNING: This article may produce Nachträglichkeit, a well-known psychoanalytic disorder in which time is made nonlinear and we rethink both what happened and what is now happening. Common symptoms: vertigo and dissociation. Best treatment: thinking and feeling one's way toward new ideas and integrations.

Trying not to psychoanalyze this gifted writer and psychoanalytic pioneer, I do wonder at the outset, after an admiring and congratulatory introduction, why Thompson gets caught up in a meditative riff on big and little. She asks, perhaps somewhat anxiously: Can she speak about belonging? Is she up to the demanding title of her talk? Can we answer that question here and now? Who else could write such a lecture?

From the beginning of this article, I have felt mindful that this is an extraordinary voice. By her own description, sometimes heretical, sometimes determined keeper of the flame, sometimes score settling, Thompson does what we have all done in this field, namely to write a birth narrative. Sometimes it's a story of migration and exile, sometimes of arrival and triumph, sometimes both. We start the story somewhere and where we start is a powerful organizing force to where we go and how we tell the story.

In reading the “History of the William Alanson White Institute,” delivered by Clara Thompson in 1955, I felt a deep sense of gratitude to Donnel Stern for bringing us the voice of a treasured founder, a psychoanalytic leader. I had much earlier discovered the works of Clara Thompson for their liberating feminist criticisms and for elucidating a two-person psychology with an increased attentiveness to the analyst's subjective and idiosyncratic presence, but that was early on my journey to become a psychoanalyst.

A couple of years ago, I found myself enchanted—I think that is the best way to describe my feelings—again with this bold psychoanalyst. The fact that she too loved the Outer Cape and the freedom of Provincetown became a fascination. I interviewed analysts who knew her and who also summered on the Cape about their experiences with her in this unique community. Not only did I unashamedly feel I shared something with her—certainly, my love of the Cape—but my attraction to her seemed further fueled by the notion that she brought a sexual liberation into the analytic discourse that was still largely unarticulated and certainly not attributed to her. Megan Kolano   Megan Kolano, Psy.D., is a clinical psychologist and postdoctoral psychology fellow at the Austen Riggs Center. 25 Main Street PO Box 962 Stockbridge, MA 01262 megan.kolano@austenriggs.net

A prolific writer, researcher, and cognitive neuroscientist, William R. Uttal has written over 20 books on the brain sciences over the last 40 years, and he has done so in atypical fashion. To the surprise of the psychologically savvy but neuroscientifically naïve, a quick scan of his Amazon page reveals interesting title phrases that pop out and pique curiosity—phrases like “Psychomythics,” “Phrenology,” “Against Behavioral Reductionism,” and “Dualism: The Original Sin of Cognitivism.” Immediately challenging the neuroscientist stereotype with his languages of philosophy and mind, Uttal's writing is easily accessible and almost instantly disarming, particularly to those who might be wary of neuroreductionism. Like a true scientist, Uttal persistently strives to move closer to understanding the neuronal components of mentation; however, he does so knowing that this problem might not be solvable. He further takes a philosophy of science approach in this pursuit, asking the epistemological question of how do we know what we think we know, all the while maintaining a healthy suspicion of knowledge as such. In his commitment to unpacking the very process of investigation used in his inquiry, Uttal reveals the mythologies and artifacts that guide curiosity and shape conclusions while also inviting his readers to be equally critical and cautious research consumers.

Steven H. Cooper's The Analyst's Experience of the Depressive Position: The Melancholic Errand of Psychoanalysis is an important and captivating read. Through his presentation of vivid case material and the theoretical issues these cases illuminate, the author highlights vitally important issues relating to pluralism in contemporary psychoanalysis and demonstrates how these issues will affect the future of psychoanalytic theory and technique. According to Cooper, no version of psychoanalysis provides a unique theoretical panacea that might solve all the clinical dilemmas of modern practice. Further, the majority of clinical problems can be justifiably formulated from different theoretical systems and most contemporary analytic practice is probably based on hybrid theory. Cooper demonstrates this phenomenon in his own work, which conveys the interplay of different traditions. He primarily explores American relational theory, the Kleinian approach, and the Independent tradition, asking all the while: is it really possible to amalgamate concepts from these different traditions? If so, how is it accomplished?

For Cooper, the key to moving beyond pluralism is the adoption of the depressive position. Although he takes this concept from the Kleinian school, his focus is not in examining the Kleinian conception of the depressive position and its complex relation with aggression, reparation, etc. Rather, he suggests that it is the acceptance of loss of the ideal that is essential for any umbrella theory of the analytic process. Larry was dead; Brandon had shot him. The murder trial, in which not a single material fact was ever in dispute, took three years of pretrial preparation, and a full two months of testimony from 98 witnesses, almost all of which was aimed solely at determining motive. From the book's inside flap: “In February 2008, during first period English class at a junior high school in Oxnard, California, blue-eyed and blond fourteen-year-old Brandon McInerney shot and killed fifteen-year-old Larry King, a brown boy, who had recently begun to identify as Leticia.”

Brandon confessed to police at the scene; in fact, he had killed Larry right in front of his homeroom teacher and 26 classmates. The only question was why. Who, what, where, and when were known, but motive consumed the trial and, accordingly, the book.

Ken Corbett, psychologist, psychoanalyst, author, and academic, is an expert on boyhood and gender, including modern-day takes on masculinity, male and female stereotypes, gender identity, and social norms. He also works clinically with transgender youth. He was intrigued by this Note to the Reader: I have used “Larry” and “he” in this article, rather than “Leticia” and “she,” because “Larry” was the language of the courtroom, the court record, and the book. I did so even though, as author Ken Corbett noted, doing so means that history will remember the story this way, with Leticia not fully “named” and her transgender identity not fully recognized, which is in itself a kind of repetitive denial of “Leticia” herself. Corbett did attempt in places to use “Leticia,” mostly when writing from her perspective, in an effort to recognize her account of herself, and I have followed the author's lead where practical.441

The relationship between psychoanalysis and literature dates from Sigmund Freud's remark, in Studies on Hysteria (1893/1955, pp. 160–161), that he still found it strange that his case histories “should read like short stories … and that they lack the serious stamp of science” but that they nonetheless had the advantage over psychiatric ones of relating the story of the patient's sufferings to the symptoms of his illness. A few years later, in The Interpretation of Dreams (Freud, 1900/1953, pp. 261-264), his analysis of one mythical story, that of Oedipus, was to provide him with the most important theme in the psychoanalytic theory of emotional and sexual development. The psychoanalytic community is almost uniformly left-leaning. That homogeneity fosters a sense of moral community and belongingness but limits the theoretical and clinical grasp of issues with powerful emotional valence among right-leaning patients. In addition, the lack of friction within the community can discourage inquiry into the unconscious loyalties and personal experiences that shape political sentiments, both left and right. In ordinary times (anytime besides say, now or the Civil War), that limitation would invite disinterested attention to the process by which political beliefs and actions form within the individual. In the time of Trump, however, that dispassionate remove feels like moral negligence to those on the left. The tension between analysts' clinical and partisan identities therefore, clearly tilts toward the latter.

Using the work of the Botellas (2005), Laplanche (1999), and Levine (2012), I aim to examine unconscious communications between patient and clinician and the transformational process that moves intersubjectively from unrepresented toward represented mental states. During my work with Sea, sessions from my own analysis revealed content that I failed to recognize as my own; unconscious untranslatable messages given to me by her that were half understood during my supervision, and crystalized only during my own analysis. Using my own changes in representational states that became available to me during this shifting of positions, I worked as Sea's “double,” sharing with her my ability to consolidate her internal representations, while strengthening her ability to reflect in the face of potentially self-destructive actions. Weaving in my own analysis with our therapy sessions, I show how regressive states from the clinician create the potential place from which the patient can form his or her own representations of that which had formerly remained un-representable because of traumatic origins. I discuss the ways in which this process might be multi-directional.

For decades, psychoanalysis has focused on the study of intrapsychic experience, but increasingly analysts are turning to neuroscience as a mode of understanding our internal worlds. Although this focus has been bolstered by recent advances in neurobiological research, the endeavor itself is not entirely new as even Freud, at least initially, also hoped to reconcile his understanding of metapsychology with neurological science in his early work, Project for a Scientific Psychology (Freud, 1895/1950). In The Neuropsychology of the Unconscious, Efrat Ginot, an instructor at the Institute for Contemporary Psychotherapy, who has written and lectured on the relationship between psychoanalytic and neurobiological understandings of the mind, joins this renewed focus. She sets out to explain the neurobiological underpinnings of unconscious mental processes, particularly those that might underlie intractable psychological problems. In her words, “Why are emotional and behavioral difficulties so pernicious, enduring, stubborn and repetitive even when we gain insight and are determined to change them?” (p. xxxi). Accordingly, in addition to summarizing much neurobiological literature, she attempts to apply it to complex clinical phenomena, including narcissism, the intergenerational transmission of trauma, and the nature of the psychotherapeutic process.

Barri Belnap   Barri Ann Belnap is a psychoanalyst and psychotherapist at the Austen Riggs Center. barribelnap@gmail.com

The great naturalist Alexander von Humboldt, trying to categorize the animals he was studying, is reported to have cried out in frustration 607 “if only they would stop and open their mouths so we can count their teeth!” Were we to emulate the energy and discipline of 19th-century naturalists in their efforts to categorize nature's expression of herself, we would study the many types of psychoses in their environments. In Bollas's recent book, When the Sun Bursts: The Enigma of Schizophrenia, he does just this for our young science of psychosis. He details for us psychosis's expressions in individuals, in the culture, and in specific historical moments. More importantly, he invites us to follow the life of psychosis in a few individuals who open themselves up for detailed appreciation of their internal world and the personal histories they are creating as they live among us.

Frieda Fromm-Reichmann wrote, “loneliness is one of the least satisfactorily conceptualized psychological phenomena” (Fromm-Reichmann, 1990, p. 306). Speaking of the “disintegrative loneliness” that “leads ultimately to psychotic states,” she asks, “What has gone wrong in the history of the lonely ones?” (Fromm-Reichmann, 1990, p. 309). The stories in Bollas's book provide answers, and the first principles of his technique address Fromm-Reichmann's question directly.

Loneliness is one of the bridges that Bollas employs to invite readers into the rich worlds of his patients. It is difficult not to become deeply curious about their minds. We discover that they see things about our shared world that are not so foreign and alien as we might expect. The psychotic's effort to engage loneliness reflects meanings embedded in the patient's life history in ways that could not be predicted. Although loneliness is a common thread in psychosis, it is at the same time singular, particular to the patient and his or her life story.

Bollas's presentation of case material sheds light on his success with often recalcitrant-seeming psychosis. His descriptions are nuanced and respectful; he respects the loneliness his psychotic patients endure and seeks to understand it at deep and painful—for himself as well as the patient—levels. Of course, this seems obvious, but Bollas reminds us of it in an experiential way. His work is a profound example of what is most psychoanalytic: respect for the unique nature of each person as reflected in his or her experiences and the language used to communicate those experiences.

Feminism and the role and rights of women became a central theme of the 2016 presidential election. Trump, since taking office, has acted in ways that directly and adversely affect women. One issue that unites both the women who voted for and those who voted against Trump is the conviction that the world has become a threatening, dangerous, and treacherous place. What is, or could be, the unique contribution of psychoanalysis to this dangerous political climate? What we do have to offer is our expertise as listeners, our ability to hold opposing and even contradictory views in mind simultaneously and our ability to maintain an attitude of neutrality. As such, we are in a position to facilitate dialogue between groups and individuals who have become polarized. Without dialogue, splits become even more extreme and those on the “other side” are increasingly vilified, their views exaggerated.

When I entered the White Institute in 1951, Clara Thompson was its primary luminary and spokesperson. Sullivan had died in 1949 while attending a meeting in Paris. Erich Fromm had moved to Mexico City where he started his eponymous institute. I do not know how much his teachings there were devoted to his own work and how much to an interpersonal psychoanalytic perspective. He did, however, come frequently to New York, and I did have the opportunity to attend his classes and group supervision. I had personal supervision with Clara for several years and consider her the major influence on my thinking at that time. After she died in 1958, the Institute nearly collapsed until it was rescued by Earl Witenberg's directorship that—albeit authoritarian—brought us to our present building and renown.

Clara's major influences were, of course, Freud, Sullivan, and Ferenczi, and she taught an amalgam of these sometimes incompatible masters. From Freud came a relatively neutral, nonintrusive approach, and a belief in the reality and clinical relevance of the unconscious in both participants. On one occasion, she said to me that “the trouble with some White [Institute] people is that they don't believe in the unconscious!” From Ferenzci came her great respect for the integrity of the patient, for symptoms as partial solutions, and for a deep-felt egalitarianism. From Sullivan came the importance of contagious anxiety and the relevance of the patient's sociocultural matrix.1 Perhaps Fromm was an important reinforcement of Sullivan's emphasis on the real life of the patient in a manifest world. Janina Sochaczewski MA

Janina Sochaczewski

Janina Sochaczewski   Janina Sochaczewski, M.A., is a doctoral student in the Department for the Study of Religion at the University of Toronto.Address correspondence to Janina Sochaczewski, M.A., 170 St. George Street, Toronto, ON M5R 2M8, Canada. E-mail: janina.sochaczewski@mail.utoronto.ca
psychoanalysis, Ian Barbour, religion, modernity, postmodernity, secularism

Using Ian Barbour's fourfold typology of the relationship between religion and science—Conflict, Independence, Dialogue, and Integration—this article examines how the relationship between religion and psychoanalysis has increasingly moved from being one of perceived irreducible Conflict to one in which Dialogue and—even in some cases— Integration are attempted and valued. Examination of the evolving relationship between religion and psychoanalysis allows for corollary discussion of how the effects of religion on modernity may be understood via a psychoanalytic lens. Although sociopolitical models are often used in studying secularism and the implications of modernity and postmodernity for religion, psychoanalytic investigation offers an alternative perspective on how modern individuals experience religion. Further, this article aims to demonstrate how the epistemological changes that have affected religion and the field of religious studies have also contributed to the reinterpretation and reconstruction of the classical psychoanalytic view of religion.

Sometimes a piece of writing so takes my breath away that, feeling awed, I have to shut the book and ask of the writer: “How did you just do that?” How in the world did you figure out how to choose those words and put them in that order in such a way that made me taste cinnamon, smell pine, or do whatever it was that this writing so magically did? With psychoanalytic writing, I might ask, how was a patient conjured with so much palpable texture that whatever defines this person—her sulk, her gaze, her impatience—is made so vivid and alive? I bet this is a familiar experience for Suzi Naiburg, who has written an almost empirical book about the experience of admiring and trying to understand the writing of others. Didactic, deeply researched, and written with a determination to understand clinical writing by systematically unpacking it, Structure and Spontaneity in Clinical Prose is a culminating volume of ideas for Naiburg, who has spent a career immersed in the teaching of clinical writing. The book will be of interest to both beginning and seasoned clinical writers.

Writing exercises—drills set off from the page in boxes outlined in black—are interspersed throughout the book. They have a distinct “here's one way to do it; now you try” feel. The exercises are not only teacherly tools, they provoke implicit and challenging questions about the utility and limitations of such drills. Among them, in the broadest sense, is the question of how and whether art can be taught, and, more narrowly, what happens when it is not just any writing that is the focus of scrutiny, but psychoanalytic writing that is under consideration, since psychoanalysis itself rests on learning from the inside–out rather than the outside–in. If an analysis proper—its trajectory and end-product—cannot be forecasted or scripted, how, one is left to ask, is psychoanalytic writing any more conducive to being architected from the outset? I will comment briefly on these questions at the end of this review, after summarizing the contents of the book and discussing its contributions to the canon of writing about writing.

The author considers the “ideals” of masculinity for boys and men and the potential for these ideals (in their extremity) to contribute to rigid psychic states and splitting. Split-off parts can return through “gremlin-like” symptoms. These symptoms are subjectively experienced as trouble making, particularly in relation to being “big” or “macho,” physically or intellectually. This case study recounts the first years of an analysis that began as therapy for depression but rapidly shifted its focus to promoting coconsciousness and cooperation among personalities who were discovered to be comprising a rigidly dissociated sense of self. At first, unusual ways of experiencing the world were only hinted at, but as the treatment progressed, acute pain and confusion surfaced—both during sessions and in the events and artwork brought to them—revealing a perplexing realm in which facts could be invented accidentally and logic was a threat. patriarchy, attachment theory, gender development, rupture and repair, voice, resistance

This article brings psychoanalysis to the fore in grappling with the question: Why does patriarchy persist? It highlights the psychological function of patriarchy as a defense against loss by connecting Gilligan's research on development with Bowlby's studies of attachment. Pathological responses to loss parallel the gender codes of patriarchal masculinity and femininity, which are internalized through an initiation that forces ruptures in relationship and subverts the capacity for repair. This parallel suggests that the gender roles, which uphold a patriarchal order, simultaneously defend against the loss of connection inherent in that order. Does being a psychoanalyst imply that one should hold a particular political sensibility? This article aims to approach this question in the aftermath of Donald Trump having become the president of the United States and the reverberations of this event, both political and personal, in analytic spaces. Contemplating the ways in which psychoanalysis addresses (or not) the social and political aspects of life, I argue that the social is the unconscious of the unconscious of psychoanalysis. The social is the unconscious of the unconscious of psychoanalysis in the sense that, unlike the unconscious that it traditionally assumes and aims to uncover—the unconscious of drives, of object relations, and of family life—psychoanalysis is reluctant to attend, both in theory and in practice, to the social forces that structure our very being and underwrite our lives. It is so reluctant that one might argue that the social is repressed into an even deeper unconscious, one that disappears completely out of sight. I suggest in the article that the reason for this reluctance is our collective historic trauma, as a discipline created by displaced people and refugees. And I try to imagine what might be our subject matter if psychoanalysis moves beyond its avoidance of the social.

The coincidence of hearing two different patients describe watching the same reality television show as a way of comforting themselves during the 2016 election campaign leads the author to reflect on how this particular show came to occupy the place of thirdness in ongoing sessions. Thinking together about this reality show added a new dimension that made it possible for patient and therapist to emerge from a merged state of disbelief into an exploration of the meaning of what seemed an unimaginable political reality, and the exercise of individual agency. In the second part of the article, the author reviews the unfortunate history that has frequently emerged when psychoanalytic institutions attempt to coexist with totalitarian regimes. Many, including the author and his patients, are reacting to Trump's election and the ongoing realities of his presidency with feelings of outrage and betrayal: How could the country have elected this man? It has been 73 years since Clara Thompson told us how the William Alanson White Institute was conceived out of conflict, born in adversity, raised in poverty, and reared in the wilderness. The rebels, the mavericks, the outsiders, and, of course, the rejected of the psychoanalytic world found shelter and nourishment within this new community. The psychoanalytic establishment was first critical, then disdainful, and over time tried to ignore or deny its existence. The Institute thrived in isolation, carving a niche, spawning several generations of radical thinkers. Many of its insights seeped into the mainstream, eventually revolutionizing psychoanalytic practice and theory.1 After seven decades of tentative contacts, moving forward and back, closer and away, the White community was invited to the establishment table, to become members of the American Psychoanalytic Association. Reluctant, skeptical, but flattered, willing to partner but unwilling to compromise its independence or integrity, the membership finally agreed to join in 2015.

What a pleasure to return to Clara Thompson's pithy description of our institutional and organizational roots. And to realize that in these many years not so much has changed. Hilit Brodsky PHD

Hilit Brodsky

Hilit Brodsky   Hilit Erel-Brodsky, Ph.D., is a psychoanalyst and a member of the Israeli Psychoanalytic Society and a lecturer at the TAU University and the BIU University.Address correspondence to Hilit Brodsky, Ph.D. E-mail: hilitbr@gmail.com
secrets, supervision, unthinkable thoughts, training process, triangle, third party in supervision

Supervision as part of a training process is triadic more than dyadic and is based on multiple triangles that can include the supervisor, the student, the academic institution, and the patient as potential vertices (Arlow, 1963; Baudry, 1993; Berman, 2000; Ekstein & Wallerstein, 1958; Gediman & Wolkenfeld, 1980; Teitelbaum, 1998). From the first meeting of the supervisor–student—analogous to the mother–baby relationship—there is a third party present, the academic institution. The third party provides space and security, marking boundaries of time and defining the extent and nature of the relationship. At the same time, the third party may give rise to feelings of exposure, guilt, and shame. In this triangle, one of the parties often withholds information, or two parties share information to which the third party is not privy. I suggest that during the process of supervision, information that has become a secret may become a “blind spot,” infringing on the movement throughout the supervision and on the ability to think freely.

dissociation, neoliberalism, “doer and done-to,” the Third, mass psychology, shame

In this article the author draws connections between the current political situation in the United States and other historical moments in which mass movements with authoritarian tendencies played a significant role. Her thesis is that psychoanalytic thinking can contribute to understanding this profoundly anti-democratic constellation in terms of the core fantasy of “only one can live.” This fantasy supports the polarity between Them and Us, in which a discardable, devalued subjugated group is seen to be a threat to the self-proclaimed dominant group. She argues that, historically, the United States has been riven by the contradiction between the democratic values of equality and social solidarity and the ideology that tries to justify harming others in the name of self-preservation, not only in slavery but also in the capitalist system of extracting profit from others' labor. The latest version of this anti-democratic ideology, neoliberalism, has colluded in denying the harm being done to our nominal democracy, or to the many, by the oligarchic concentration of power in the hands of the wealthy who profit from this system. She aims to elucidate the psychic forces that enable the dissociation of this harming and those that might contribute to exposing the threat to democracy and, through acknowledging the history of harming, engage in repair.

referral source, referral, first session, therapist's self-interest, countertransference, supervision

Myriad factors influence the initial phase of treatment. Among these, the impact of the referral source and what transpires during the referral process is a neglected area. The patient, therapist, and referral source will inevitably introduce their unique selves into dynamic interactions. This article focuses on the experiences of the therapist. Several factors, including economic and personal ones, contribute to how vulnerable a therapist will be to the ubiquitous pull of self-interest. In addition, the thinking and behavior of each participant—patient, therapist, referral source—may be further shaped by the contextual fields within which these individuals exist and in which treatment takes place. The term “referral matrix” is proposed to capture the dynamic interplay of the constellation of factors within and surrounding the three participants, which may manifest at conscious and unconscious levels. Case studies are presented to demonstrate how the various influences can intertwine. The author discusses clinical situations when, due to heightened self-interest, therapists alter their usual modes of listening and responding to patients. These shifts can result in a diffusion of boundaries among all the participants and a greater tendency for enactments to take place. Frequently encountered countertransference reactions are discussed, as well as the implications of the referral matrix for supervision.

LGBTQ, Trump, psychoanalysis, civil rights, projection, distortion, social conservative

During the early days of the campaign and Trump administration, popular opinion suggested that the threat to LGBTQ civil rights achievements posed by a Trump administration would be minimal, given Trump's lack of explicit anti-LGBTQ animus. This optimism has been tested. In this article, I argue that, in fact, the potential destructive effect on LGBTQ rights is real but that detecting it requires an appreciation for unconscious projection and distortion. Donald Trump may at times espouse LGBTQ rights with his words, but through his deeds and associations with social conservative groups—who contain and act out his disavowed anti-LGBTQ hostility—he communicates an unconscious message of rejection and hate. Such mystification mirrors what LGBTQ individuals have often encountered in their upbringings and poses insidious threats to our basic security and self-worth. Psychoanalysts are well-positioned for decoding such mixed messages, and it behooves us as a field to bring our skills to bear on the effects of these messages, particularly on LGBTQ youth.

This is the story of the early years of my therapeutic work with my patient, Adam—a young man who, as I came to see it, probed actively in order to assess my capacity for what I would call realness, reciprocity, and presence. My empathy seemed to depend in good part on how Adam saw and read my inner experience of myself and of him, as well as on how I experienced being seen and known by him. In the process of facilitating inner change for him, we both became engaged around the same basic set of universal, human, existential issues.

My aim is to bring my readers, into my lived experience of beginning a treatment like this one—what it feels like and means to me. Adam, my patient, has seen this version of our story and chose to put his experience of our work in a recent letter you will find included after my narrative.

Each of us is likely to have at least one “Achilles' heel”—an element of selfhood that is inherently weak and deficient relative to other elements within ourselves, and to the capabilities we regularly see in others. Psychoanalytic theory has given short shrift to the painful psychic impact of these actual (as opposed to only subjectively experienced) flaws and deficits. Society often downplays, “airbrushes,” or averts its eyes from an individual's evident deficiencies; but their very existence—not to mention their impact—can evoke underlying shame and create extensive difficulties for the individual.

This article explores the ways one's Achilles' heels may have a micro-traumatic effect (Crastnopol, 2015) on oneself and others. The author discusses various constructive attitudes and approaches to grappling with ingrained flaws and limitations in the course of psychoanalytic work.

Interpersonal psychoanalysis is not well known outside the northeastern United States, yet it has been present since the 1930s and has influenced psychoanalysis all over the world. In this article, the origins of interpersonal psychoanalysis are described, providing at least a partial explanation for this widespread ignorance. Interpersonal psychoanalysis no longer finds much of its definition by an opposition to ego psychology, as it did in its early days. Today, instead, the more significant question for interpersonal psychoanalysis is how, and whether, it can be differentiated from relational psychoanalysis. This is especially important for those who, like me, identify as both interpersonal and relational. Interpersonal thinking was the heart of Mitchell's original conception of relational psychoanalysis. I argue that interpersonal psychoanalysis remains a coherent psychoanalytic perspective, defined by radical field theory; a deemphasis on unconscious fantasy and repressed memories as templates for conscious experience; an emphasis on fantasy as mystified experience; a correspondingly greater emphasis on the embeddedness of the past in the forms of the present; and most of all, the continuous, unconscious, mutual influence of the subjectivities of analyst and patient on one another.

There is a growing consensus among political analysts examining the relative roles of race, gender, class, and economic anxiety in the 2016 presidential contest: the race was about race. But the plot of Trump's delivery to the White House thickens when read through a psychoanalytic lens, with an eye to the primal scene and to anatomical difference. One key thread of the plot is the birtherism narrative and its chain of signifiers, which I argue form a complex of various “isms,” including classism, nationalism, fundamentalism, climate denialism, racism, and sexism. This complex is centered around our literal birthplace—the vagina—but it is an obscured center. I suggest that the vagina operated as a secret key to both the presidential campaign and to the Trump presidency. Though ignored in conventional analysis, this key provides crucial insight into Trump's obliviousness to reality and truth, his misogynistic actions to dismantle women's (reproductive) rights and environmental protections, and his inability to concede to the reality that he and a black man, Barack Obama, shared a common birthplace and birthright.

Pascal Sauvayre   Pascal Sauvayre,Ph.D., is faculty and a supervising analyst at the William Alanson White Institute; he is also an Executive Editor for Contemporary Psychoanalysis. He has a private practice in New York City.

Another biography of Freud? And a translation no less? Why? Could we expect any surprising reveals that might be relevant to his work, to his historical status, or even to the historical Freud known to us? In fact, Roudinesco takes a middle-of-the-road approach, on the one hand debunking the more sensationalistic “revelations” that “Freud bashing” (Roudinesco, 2016, p. 423) revels in,1 and on the other hand making a point of covering the more problematic cases (such as the Frink case), some of the odder aspects of his thought (e.g., his belief in theories doubting Shakespeare's authorship) that the more hagiographic biographies pass over in silence (Jones's opus is the prototype for that end of the spectrum).

One of the key aims of her sober, even-handed approach is to counterbalance the excesses of Freud bashing. “The theses of the ‘Freud bashers' … helped interject into public opinion a blurred image of Freud's life and work, an image sometimes based on the wildest rumors, which were presented in print as established truths. moral injury, PTSD, Trump, trauma, betrayal, leadership

The results of the 2016 U.S. presidential election came as a shock to many people, seemingly an impossible outcome. Rather than furthering the advancement of a progressive, inclusive society, the election of Donald Trump promised to further a reactionary agenda, with promises to undo what many considered long-delayed positive changes toward a kinder, more compassionate society. In addition to precipitating disbelief and terror, the election outcome and subsequent events are arguably experienced as moral injuries. In this article, the construct of moral injury is discussed alongside familiar conceptions of trauma, in an effort to enhance our understanding of how social and political changes affect people.

Clara Mabel Thompson, M.D. (18931958), whose photograph appears on page 1, was one of the founders of the William Alanson White Institute in 1946 and served as its first director until her death. She was a political activist in psychoanalysis and one of the first psychoanalytic feminists. Shapiro (2002) describes Thompson and Karen Horney, Thompson's friend and colleague, as the first psychoanalytic feminist theorists. Thompson was also an innovator in other ways, eventually bearing a significant degree of responsibility for the establishment of interpersonal psychoanalysis as a school of thought. Thompson, who knew well both Harry Stack Sullivan and Erich Fromm (she was particularly close to Sullivan), two of the other founders of White, saw that Sullivan's interpersonal relations (Sullivan's favored description of his way of thinking) could be combined with Fromm's culturalist orientation, his psychoanalytic views (Fromm was trained at the Berlin Institute), and his existentialist commitment to authenticity and spontaneity in clinical practice to shape what came to be called interpersonal psychoanalysis. It is fitting that the phrase interpersonal psychoanalysis was coined as the title of Thompson's selected papers (Thompson, 1964) by the editor of those papers, Maurice Green. Gideon Lev PHD

Gideon Lev

Gideon Lev   Gideon Lev, Ph.D., works in a private practice in Haifa, Israel. His second book, Truth, Love, Faith: Historical and psychoanalytic perspectives on the meaning of life, is to be published soon.Address correspondence to Gideon Lev, Ph.D., Neve Shaanan 25c, Jerusalem 93708, Israel E-mail: giddylev@gmail.com
psychoanalysis and spirituality, psychoanalytic technique, countertransference love, essence of psychoanalysis, the analytic experience, free association and meditation

Psychoanalysis is commonly considered a procedure for investigating the mind, a treatment method, and a general theory of mind. This article suggests that psychoanalysis can also satisfy criteria for another, less conventional, framing. Engaging with analysts' accounts, I demonstrate that psychoanalysis is a practice that deals with the most profound questions of life, creates shifts in the way reality is perceived, and even enables unconditional love to arise in the hearts of its practitioners. It can thus be deemed a mode of spiritual practice. Thanks to the recent “spiritual turn” in society, the spirituality inherent in psychoanalysis is now being acknowledged more openly. Yet the argument here is that psychoanalysis was always spiritual in essence, and it is only that today we are able to recognize this.
